title: Edge-Orientation Entropy Predicts Preference for Diverse Types of Man-Made Images
research_questions: Is edge-orientation entropy associated with aesthetic preference in a wide variety of man-made visual patterns and scenes?
How does edge-orientation entropy relate to curvilinearity in predicting aesthetic preference?
What are the relative contributions of curvilinearity and edge-orientation entropy to aesthetic ratings?
hypotheses: Edge-orientation entropy is a predictor for aesthetic ratings in at least some man-made visual stimuli.
Human observers prefer a high degree of edge-orientation entropy in more complex visual stimuli, including photographs of man-made objects and scenes.
Edge-orientation entropy and curvilinearity share predicted variance of preference for visual stimuli.
Curved stimuli will be rated more highly than angular patterns.
Stimuli with high 2nd-order entropy will be rated more highly than stimuli with low 2nd-order entropy.

methodology.participants: 20-31 participants per experiment (total 147 unique participants across experiments 2,3,5,6; Experiment 1 and 4 used existing data). Mostly university students/graduates, younger than 40 years, normal/corrected-to-normal vision, no art professionals.
methodology.stimuli: Six sets of man-made images: 1) Simple irregular geometric shapes (curved/angular, N=180); 2) Artificial ornamental patterns (Taprats, N=100); 3) Photographs of building facades (N=50); 4) Interior architectural scenes (N=200); 5) Music album covers (classic, pop, metal, N=150); 6) Complex line stimuli (angular/curved, systematically varied in 2nd-order entropy, N=100).

objective_image_properties: 2nd-order edge-orientation entropy (independence of edge orientations, calculated for 20-240 pixels and >240 pixels distances)
Edge density (sum of Gabor filter responses, related to complexity)
Openness of space (binary: open/closed) for Experiment 4
Music genre (categorical: metal, pop, classic) for Experiment 5

methodology.analysis: Multiple linear regression (lm package in R) to predict aesthetic ratings from image properties. R² and adjusted R² values, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), standardized regression coefficients (βi), t-values, and p-values were reported. ANOVA (R² difference test) for model comparisons. Mann-Whitney U test for entropy differences between curved/angular stimuli.

findings.quote: A similar relation was obtained for 2nd-order entropy (median: 4.26 and 4.15, respectively; U = 674, p = 0.0001).

findings.quote: our findings suggest that the two measures of entropy together predict the preference ratings of the stimuli about as well as their curved/angular shape

findings.mechanism: The magnitude of the effect of edge-orientation entropy on aesthetic ratings depends on image category, range of entropy values, and type of aesthetic rating.
findings.quote: The magnitude of this effect, however, depends on the category of images analyzed, on the range of entropy values encountered, and on the type of aesthetic ratings (pleasing, interesting, or harmonious).

findings.antecedent: Higher edge-orientation entropies (covering a wide range and not approaching upper bound)
findings.mechanism: A wider distribution of edge orientations, especially when not saturated, is generally preferred.
findings.quote: In general, higher edge-orientation entropies correlate with higher aesthetic rating, in particular, if entropy values cover a wide range and do not approach their upper bound.

findings.mechanism: Entropies can partly operationalize and substitute for curvilinearity in predicting aesthetic ratings, suggesting shared variance.
findings.source: General Discussion, Differences Between the Image Properties and How They Affect the Ratings
findings.quote: for most of the ratings in Experiments 1, 4, and 6, the entropies can substitute for the curvilinearity variable (shape or contour), at least in part, to predict the aesthetic ratings.

limitations: Findings are specific to the laboratory setting.
Analysis was restricted to six special types of man-made images, limiting generalizability.
Aesthetic ratings can be domain-specific, requiring further study for generalization to other man-made or natural patterns/scenes.
Participants were undergraduates or recent graduates, all younger than 40 years, potentially introducing idiosyncratic taste effects, especially for images with cultural content.
The study focused on group-level differences, not addressing inter-individual variability in preference for high edge-orientation entropy.

paper_metadata.title: Progress in Joint-Action Research
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Humans have a striking ability to coordinate their actions with each other to achieve joint goals. The tight interpersonal coordination that characterizes joint actions is achieved through processes that help with preparing for joint action as well as processes that are active while joint actions are being performed. To prepare for joint action, partners form representations of each other’s actions and tasks and the relation between them. This enables them to predict each other’s upcoming actions, which, in turn, facilitates coordination. While performing joint actions, partners’ coordination is maintained by (a) monitoring whether individual and joint outcomes correspond to what was planned, (b) predicting partners’ action parameters on the basis of familiarity with their individual actions, (c) communicating task-relevant information unknown to partners in an action-based fashion, and (d) relying on coupling of predictions through dense perceptual-information flow between coactors. The next challenge for the field of joint action is to generate an integrated perspective that links coordination mechanisms to normative, evolutionary, and communicative frameworks.

stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Typically 2-5 seconds per image, or self-paced
control_conditions: Images with varying levels of Edge-Orientation Entropy (EOE)
Comparison of simple geometric shapes (curved vs. angular)
Comparison of different categories of man-made images (e.g., architecture, objects, abstract patterns)
Comparison with natural images (in some experiments)

instruments_used.name: Preference rating scale
instruments_used.description: Likert-type scale (e.g., 1-7 or 1-9 points) used by participants to rate how much they liked or preferred each image.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Edge-Orientation Entropy (EOE) as a predictor of aesthetic preference
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Edge-Orientation Entropy (EOE), a measure of the statistical distribution of edge orientations in an image, predicts aesthetic preference for diverse types of man-made images, with intermediate levels of EOE being preferred.
The human visual system processes visual information, and aesthetic preference is influenced by an optimal level of visual complexity or order, which EOE is hypothesized to capture.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that Edge-Orientation Entropy (EOE) quantifies a fundamental aspect of visual complexity. An intermediate level of EOE is hypothesized to be optimally processed by the visual system, leading to a positive aesthetic experience and higher preference ratings.

steps.from_construct: Image properties (e.g., distribution of edge orientations)

steps.to_construct: Efficient visual processing / Positive aesthetic experience

steps.from_construct: Efficient visual processing / Positive aesthetic experience

stimulus_images.description: Examples of simple geometric shapes (e.g., circles, squares, triangles, polygons) with varying degrees of curvature and angularity.
